segments.voice: Yesterday: the Prophet, peace be upon him, al-Amin, the trustworthy. Now the whole camp, quickly: bismillah, al-Fatiha, wudu, inshallah, iman, Ramadan, Eid, salaam, the five pillars, salat, alhamdulillah, Rabb, rahma, yawm ad-din, tawhid, as-sirat al-mustaqim, the adhan, Jumu'ah, zakat, the Prophet. Twenty words. Today makes twenty-one.

Twenty words: the everyday vocabulary of a Muslim life. That's the foothills. Tomorrow the path starts climbing, into the stories of the prophets, one after another. So today, from the top of the foothills, look up at the mountain itself, the Qur'an, and find the place where almost every Muslim starts to climb it. Oddly enough, it's at the very end.
screen: `THE FOOTHILLS, DONE.` → `THE MOUNTAIN AHEAD.` → `START AT THE END.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an has a hundred and fourteen surahs, roughly longest first, shortest last. To make it possible to read the whole thing in a month, especially in Ramadan, it's divided into thirty equal parts. Each part is a juz'. The last one is called juz' 'amma, after its very first word. Surah seventy-eight opens: “Whereof do they question one another?” In Arabic, 'amma yatasa'alun. So 'amma, whereof, names the whole part. It holds the surahs from seventy-eight to the end. Most are short, some only three or four lines, and many scholars place most of them among the earliest revelations in Mecca: vivid, rhythmic, full of oaths by the dawn, the night, the fig. And this is where children begin. Not at page one: at the back. After al-Fatiha, a child often learns an-Nas, the last surah, then al-Falaq, then al-Ikhlas, the surah of oneness from day fifteen, and on backward from there. These are the surahs most often recited in the daily prayers, for a lifetime. Grandparents and five-year-olds know the same ones by heart. For some, the climb goes on for years, until the whole Qur'an is held in memory; someone who does that is called a hafiz, a keeper. But almost everyone starts here, at the small end of the mountain.
screen: `THIRTY PARTS, FOR A MONTH.` · `'AMMA — WHEREOF DO THEY QUESTION?` · `CHILDREN START AT THE BACK.` · `THE SMALL END OF THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Think back over these three weeks. Let the words drift past: the name before a beginning, the opening, the water, the fast, the feast, the greeting, the one. Don't try to remember all of them. Just notice which one has stuck, which one came back to you on an ordinary day, in the kitchen or the car, without being asked. Hold that one word. It's yours now.
Juz' 'amma. The thirtieth part of the Qur'an, the short surahs, where nearly everyone begins. Twenty-first word, and camp one is done.
Your line: the ones every Muslim child knows. Tomorrow the path starts climbing, and the stories begin.

what a scholar hears: the parts are a reading division, not the revelation's own; the surahs run roughly longest to shortest; and many of the last part's surahs are placed among the earliest Meccan revelations.
